title.en: Ness Wins Conor the Throne of Ulster
title.zh: 內斯為科納奪得阿爾斯特王位

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. I, eBook #52963

summary.en: Ness, ambitious for her son Conor, agrees to wed King Fergus mac Roy on one condition: the sovereignty shall pass to Conor for a single year. In that year she buys the hearts of Ulster with wealth and schooling, and when Fergus demands his kingdom back, the chiefs refuse him — he has resigned it, they say, for a wife. Fergus forsakes her and goes into exile to Queen Meave in Connaught with the Black Exile at his side, swearing revenge.
summary.zh: 內斯為兒子科納謀劃王位，答應嫁給費爾古斯王——條件是王權移交科納一年。一年間她以財富收買人心、教導權術；年期既滿，費爾古斯索還王位，眾酋長卻拒絕：「為娶妻而棄國者，實已遜位。」費爾古斯拋妻出走，攜「黑色流亡者」投奔康諾特女王梅芙，立誓復仇。

sensitivity.note: The one-year regency trick is the fixed usurpation device of the Ulster cycle's opening; it frames the whole Tain (Fergus the exiled king guiding Meave's host). Fergus's rainbow-weaver's-beam sword is the cycle's great weapon lore. Coordinates are the documented Emain Macha.

passages.text: When Conor was but a lad, his mother was a widow, and there was no thought that Conor would be king. For the King of Ulster at that time was Fergus mac Roy, a powerful and noble king, whom his people loved; and though Conor was of high rank and dignity, he stood not near the throne. But his mother, Ness, was ambitious for him, and she used all her arts to bring it about that he should be called to the throne of Ulster. Ness was a handsome woman, and a woman of spirit, and in her youth she had been a warrior; and Fergus admired her, and she wrought upon him so that in the end he asked her to be his wife. She made it a condition that for one year Fergus would leave the sovereignty, and that Conor should take his place; "for," said she, "I should like to have it said that my son had been a king."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: But, as soon as Conor was king, Ness set about to win away the hearts of the people of Ulster from Fergus, and to transfer them in their allegiance to Conor. She supplied her son with wealth, which he distributed secretly among the people, buying them over to his side; and when, the year being out, Fergus demanded back the sovereignty, he found that the league formed against him was so strong that he could do nothing. They agreed that Fergus should keep his wife, if he wished, but that the kingdom should pass to Conor. And Fergus was so wrath at this, that he forsook his wife, and went with a great host of his own followers into Connaught, to take refuge with Queen Meave and with Ailill, her spouse. Now Fergus mac Roy was of great stature, a mighty man and a famous warrior, and his strength was that of a hundred heroes; and all men spoke of the sword of Fergus, which was so great and long that men said that it stretched like a rainbow or like a weaver's beam.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: Cuchulain in Shadow-Land: the Training of Scathe
title.zh: 暗影之國：斯凱瑟的訓練

region.zh: 暗影之國（象徵定位於斯凱島）

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. VII, eBook #52963

summary.en: A boy yet, Cuchulain goes out to perfect every soldierly art, first with the grim Donnell and Big-fist for a year and a day, then alone across a scorched trackless desert to the Eastern world, riding a friendly lion four days and nights over the lightless land, to find the woman-champion Scathe, daughter of Ages, King of Shadow-land, from whom alone true knightly skill can be learned — Scathach of Skye, the teacher whose feats and weapons he will carry to the fords of the Tain.
summary.zh: 尚是少年的庫丘林立志習盡武藝：先隨陰森的多涅爾與「巨拳」學藝一年一日；再獨自穿越焦黑無路的荒漠，騎友善雄獅四日四夜橫越無光之境，抵達東方世界——唯「艾格斯之女斯凱瑟」所在的暗影之國，方能傳授真正的騎士技藝。此即斯凱島的女武師斯卡薩赫，其武藝與兵器日後將伴庫丘林征戰《奪牛記》的每一處渡口。

sensitivity.note: Scathach's Shadow-land is traditionally identified with the Isle of Skye (the Cuillin hills bear her name); the friendly lion carrying the boy across the desert is a fixed marvel-guide of the tale, and the year-and-a-day term is the Irish fosterage term. Pin symbolic on Skye.

passages.text: While Cuchulain was still a little lad, but strong and brave and full of spirit, it came into his mind that he would like to go out into the world to perfect himself in every kind of soldierly art, so that he might not be behind any warrior in feats of strength and skill. He went first to the Glen of Solitude in Munster, but he did not long remain there, but returned to Ulster, to invite his companions to go with him to visit the woman-warrior Scathe who dwelt in "Shadow-land." They came at last to a dark gloomy shore where dwelt a fierce woman-warrior, Donnell the Soldierly, and her daughter, Big-fist; they knew many feats of arms, so that the three warriors stayed with them a year and a day, learning all they knew. But Cuchulain was fain to go away from them, for the darkness and the gloom of the place and the ugly deeds of Big-fist troubled him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Cuchulain was walking by the brink of the sea, when he saw close beside him, sitting on the shore, a man of enormous size, every inch of him from top to toe as black as coal: "If you want to learn true knightly skill and feats of valour, it is not here that you will learn them. Far better than she is Scathe, daughter of Ages, King of Shadow-land, who dwells in the Eastern world." And when his companions' homesick visions separated them from him, Cuchulain set out alone along the unknown road; for he was determined to reach Shadow-land, or to die in the attempt.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went on for many days over great mountains and through deep impenetrable forests, and dark, lonely glens, until he came to a wide-spreading desert and a lightless land, black and scorched and bare. Just then he saw a great beast like a lion coming out of the forest, and it made no attempt to injure him, but kept turning its side to Cuchulain, inviting him to mount; and for four days and nights they travelled thus through the dim, lightless land, until they saw a small loch and a boat on it, and boys rowing the boat backward and forward amongst the reeds of the shore, and the boys laughed at the sight of the hurtful beast doing service to a human being.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Fergus Misleads the Host and the Four-Pronged Pole
title.zh: 費爾古斯誤導大軍與四叉木柱

region.en: Ford on the Shannon borders, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭香農河畔渡口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. X, eBook #52963

summary.en: Snow falls to the chariot-wheels, and Fergus — guiding Meave's host — leads it in circles out of love for his own province, warning: the standing of Cuchulain will be as the crouching of the Hounds of War upon your path. Cuchulain cuts a four-pronged oak pole with one sweep, throws it into the stream with one hand, and impales four heads on its points; the ring on it reads that the men of Erin may not pass till it is plucked up in the same manner — and chariot after chariot of Fergus's goes to splinters.
summary.zh: 大雪沒輪，費爾古斯領軍卻因故鄉之情率軍繞圈，並警告：「庫丘林之立，猶如戰犬伏於你們的必經之途。」庫丘林一揮劍削出四叉橡木柱，單手擲入溪流中央，柱尖各插一顆人頭；柱環刻文曰：除非有人以同樣單手之力拔起此柱，愛爾蘭之軍不得過河——費爾古斯的戰車一輛輛撞得粉碎。

sensitivity.note: This is Hull's retelling of the LU withe-and-pillar passage (existing record celtic-withe-ogam-geis-host covers Faraday's recension); Hull's version has the four-pronged pole with four heads — a variant form of the geis-token, kept as a distinct recension record. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: It was in the beginning of winter that they set out, and already snow lay heavy on the ground; on the very first night it fell so thickly, that it reached to the chariot-wheels. Meave called Fergus: "Go on before the hosts, O Fergus, and find us out the shortest road into Ulster." So with a few companions Fergus went on ahead; but as he drove along, the memory of old friends and of his home and country came upon him, and an overwhelming affection for Ulster took hold on him, and in his mind there arose shame and bitter self-reproach that he, the former King of Ulster, should be leading Ulster's foes against her. So to the North and the South he misled the host, while in the meantime he sent swift messengers to Conor and the Ulster chiefs, but especially to his own foster-son Cuchulain. "Beware and look out well for your troops to-night and every night from this; for it may be that Cuchulain will stand between you and Ulster, and the standing of Cuchulain will be as the crouching of the Hounds of War upon your path."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: No sooner had Sualtach gone his way than Cuchulain entered a forest close at hand and out of an oak sapling cut a four-pronged pole, which with one sweep of his swift sword he cleared of all its twigs and leaves and small branches. With the finger-tips of his right hand he hurled it out behind his chariot, going at full pace, so that it sank into the ground in the middle of the stream, and stood up just above the water. Upon the pole he flung a ring or twisted collar of young birch, and on the ring he carved his name and a message in secret runes; and two young men of the host of Meave, gone out before the troops to scout, he slew, and their heads and the heads of their charioteers were impaled on the four points of the forked pole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It is written on the ring that with one hand this pole was thrown, and fixed firmly in its bed; it is written here, moreover, that the men of Erin are forbidden to pass this ford, until in exactly the same manner it is plucked up again." A chariot was brought and Fergus mounted into it, and though he tugged and strained, so that the chariot flew into little bits and fragments, he could not stir or move the pole an inch; one chariot after another he essayed, and all of them went into splinters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. X; not verbatim.

title.en: Nacrantal and the Nine Spits of Holly-Wood
title.zh: 納克蘭塔爾與九支冬青肉叉

region.en: Ford of challenge, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼挑戰渡口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Nacrantal, promised land and Finnabar, takes no arms but nine spits of holly-wood hardened in fire; Cuchulain, hawking, leaps over each spit as it falls. Taunted with flight, he answers that he fights only men-at-arms fully equipped — and Fergus, ashamed, sends the rebuke that turns the trick: Laeg smears a false beard with blackberry juice and sheep's wool, the battle-fury transforms the boy's face, and he carries off a pillar-stone in his mantle without knowing its weight. Nacrantal's sword breaks on the stone and one blow lays him on his own shield.
summary.zh: 受諾土地與芬娜芭爾的納克蘭塔爾僅持九支火烤冬青尖叉出戰；庫丘林正在放鷹逐鳥，逐一躍過落下的尖叉。被誣臨陣脫逃後，他答曰只與全副武裝的戰士交手——費爾古斯羞愧傳話；萊格以黑莓汁與羊毛為他做假鬚，戰怒改易其容，斗篷間竟不自覺夾起一根石柱。納克蘭塔爾之劍斷於石上，一擊斃命，倒在自己的盾上。

sensitivity.note: The false-beard trick is Hull's version of the beard-magic of the Loch episode (Faraday's record covers the Long/Loch variant); the pillar-stone caught in the mantle unnoticed is the riastrad strength-sign. The holly-spits challenge repeats the spits-of-hollywood chapter title of the Tain. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Among the chiefs was a rough burly man and a good fighter, whose name was Nacrantal, whom Meave used all her arts to force to challenge Cuchulain. And in the end, when she had promised him large gifts of land and even Finnabar, her daughter, to be his wife, he was induced to go. But even so he went not out as though to fight an equal. No arms or armour would he take, but for his sole protection nine spits of holly-wood, sharp at the points and hardened in the fire. He found the hero busied in pursuing wild-fowl that were flying overhead; for from the birds of the air and fish of the streams, and from the berries of the hedge and cresses of the brook, long had he been obliged to get his daily meal. Closer the warrior drew and with good aim he flung his spits of wood to pierce Cuchulain. But still the youth, not stopping for a moment in his task, leaped lightly over each spit as it fell, so that they struck the ground quite harmlessly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Do you and Fergus not yet understand that I, Cuchulain, fight no men unarmed, or messengers, or charioteers, but only men-at-arms, fully equipped?" Laeg took the juice of blackberries, and sheep's wool, and with it made a long two-pointed beard, such as prime warriors wore, and twined the ends and caught them in his belt, dyeing it black with juice. Then on the hero came anger and his battle-fury; a subtle change came over all his face; his stature seemed to grow, his form to enlarge, and terrible in its strength and fierceness was his aspect.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: So great his wrath and eagerness for combat, that as he passed a standing pillar-stone no smaller than himself, in flinging his mantle round him as he went he caught the stone up in his mantle's folds and carried it along with him, but never was he conscious of its weight. Then Nacrantal made a furious onset at Cuchulain with his sword, but it struck on the pillar-stone that he carried beneath his cloak, and broke off short, close to his hand; and lifting his sword on high with both hands, Cuchulain brought it down on his adversary's head, and there on his own shield he fell dead, smitten with one blow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fairy Swan-Maidens of the Plain of Delight

region.en: Lake on the Plain of Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼湖畔

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XX, eBook #52963

summary.en: At the autumn feast Cuchulain brings down birds for the women but gives none to Emer; two noble swans linked with a golden chain, chanting a mystic sleep-song, come sailing — and for the first time in his life his sling misses, his spear glances, and the wounded swan vanishes under water with Laeg asleep behind him. Two fairy women with osier switches strike his strength away: Liban, wife of Labra the Swift of Moy Mell, come to bid him welcome — the beginning of his trip to Fairy-Land.
summary.zh: 秋日盛宴，庫丘林為眾女獵鳥，卻未給埃妮德一隻；兩隻金鏈相連、吟唱催眠仙歌的貴天鵝緩緩而來——他一生中第一次失手：彈石掠過、矛刺落空、受傷的天鵝沒入水中，萊格在他身後酣睡。兩位執柳條的仙姝以杖輕點，吸走他的力氣：利巴恩——極樂平原「迅捷者」拉布拉之妻——前來相邀，仙遊之地由此開啟。

sensitivity.note: The swan-maidens are Hull's retelling of the Serglige (Sick-bed) prelude — the fairy-hostage pattern behind the Fand episode (existing record celtic-sickbed-fand covers the Fand core); the first-time-ever missed sling-shot is the tale's enchanted-capture device. Pin at Murthemne lake tradition.

passages.text: One day during an autumn feast, Cuchulain and Emer his wife were amusing themselves beside a lake, when they saw coming from a distance a flock of white, very beautiful swans, which settled down upon the lake, and began to swim out two and two. "How I wish that I could have two of those birds, one on each of my shoulders," said Emer. Cuchulain brought down a number of them with his sword and with stones, and threw them down before the women, but to Emer he gave not any birds at all. Then slowly sailing out of the far distance they saw two noble swans, larger and more splendid than any of those that had been on the lake before: the birds were chanting a gentle, mystic song, that soothed all who listened to it to sleep; and they were linked together with a golden chain.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.

passages.text: "There are your birds, O Emer," said Cuchulain, and he rose up to pursue them. But Emer was afraid: "Go not against those birds; there is some magic power in those birds, and you may come to harm." He took the sling and made a very careful aim, but for the first time in his life he missed his aim; and again the stone went past them; and he flung his spear, and it seemed as though the spear went through the swans, but the wing of one of them was broken, and they flew away unhurt, and disappeared beneath the water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.

passages.text: A strange weariness overtook him, and he leaned his back against a pillar stone, and drowsiness fell upon him. Then in a vision Cuchulain saw two graceful women approach him, clad in fairy mantles of green and purple, and they had little switches of osier in their hands, and they began to strike him gently with the rods, and it seemed to Cuchulain that all his strength departed from him while they touched him with their rods. "We are come," said the first, "out of Moy Mell, the Land of all Delight, the radiant Honey-Plain beyond the waves, to seek thy friendship. Liban am I, wife of Labra the Swift, the Wielder of the Sword, the monarch of that land."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XX; not verbatim.

title.en: Deirdre's Walled Garden and the Ball of Dreams
title.zh: 迪爾德麗的高牆花園與夢中之球

region.en: Lonely dell far from Emain Macha, Co. Armagh (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿馬郡遠離埃馬因的僻谷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XXIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Conor's jealousy of the boy-corps takes Deirdre at seven years old from the playing fields and walls her in a lonely dell behind man-hounds, where nurse Levarcam teaches her every bird and herb and star. But the memory of Naisi's mis-thrown ball — caught by the child, returned with a smile and a promise — works in her dreams: every night Conor comes between and throws it back, till one night the ball strikes Naisi red and bleeding like the sacrificed calf, and the captive bride pines for a man she may not name.
summary.zh: 科納因妒忌少年軍，將七歲的迪爾德麗帶離球場，圈入深谷高牆之內，四猛犬日夜把守；智慧乳母教她百鳥、百草與星辰。然而奈西失手拋來、她撿回並得他微笑一諾的那顆球，夜夜入夢：科納總在中途奪球擲回，直到某夜球擊中奈西——紅染如祭壇上的牛犢——被囚的新娘為一個不能說出名字的男人憔悴。

sensitivity.note: Hull's version adds the walled garden and the captive-education topos to the Deirdre birth-prophecy (existing record celtic-deirdre-exile covers the exile and death); the dream-ball sequence is Hull's omen-psychology — the future killing foreseen as a child's game. Pin symbolic near Emain.

passages.text: Then Conor called his Druid Caffa to him, and he said, "Too long we leave this child at liberty among the chieftain's sons. She must henceforth be kept apart... She shall come to me of her own free will, because she knows no other man but me. She shall not even know what kind of thing a man may be, for I will shut her up apart from men, and, save yourself and me, she shall not ever see a manly face." So for the girl he built a place apart, far off from Emain in a lonely dell, surrounded by a wood; and all seemed fair enough, but round the place he built a mighty wall, so high that none could climb it, and a moat ran round within. Four savage man-hounds sent by Conor were on constant guard, watching on every side by night and day, so that no living thing could enter or pass out, save with the knowledge of Levarcam.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And for a time the child was happy, for Levarcam, the wise woman, taught her all she knew: how each bird sings to its mate, each different note of thrush or cuckoo or the soaring lark; the plants that spring towards heaven, and of their names and uses; and in the solemn night, they went abroad and watched the motion of the stars. But the maiden drooped and pined: "Seven bitter years since I beheld the joyous playing field, and saw the sports, and marked the manly face of Naisi, noblest and bravest of the corps of boys." "He told me so, when he threw the ball, by a mis-cast, backward, across the heads of the group of maidens who were standing on the edge of the green, and I rose up among them all, picked up the ball, and gave it back to him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: He pressed my hand and smiled, and promised he would see me oft again... But in my dreams I see him every night playing at ball with me; and when he flings the ball for me to catch, 'tis ever the same thing: King Conor comes between and seizes it, and throws it back at Naisi. But last night, King Conor flung the ball craftily at his head, and Naisi fell all red and stained with blood, like that poor calf that Caffa slew."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hound at Bay against the Pillar-Stone

region.en: Ford of Cuchulain's last battle, Mag Murthemne, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭穆瑟姆尼庫丘林最後戰場（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ulster cycle, Eleanor Hull retelling, Cuchulain the Hound of Ulster (1910)

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), ch. XXVIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Fighting his last fight against Meave's geas-breaking host, Cuchulain is mortally stricken; he will not fall but goes to the pillar-stone, straps his body upright with his belt, and dies on his feet facing his foes, his hand on his weapons, so that even his enemies dare not approach until a raven — the bird of the Morrigan — comes to settle on his shoulder. The Hound at bay is the Ulster cycle's dying-standing image.
summary.zh: 與梅芙背誓之軍作最後一戰的庫丘林身負致命傷；他不肯倒下，走向石柱，以腰帶縛身直立，面向敵人手握兵器而亡——直到摩里岡的烏鴉落上他的肩頭，敵軍才敢靠近。「困守之犬」是阿爾斯特史詩「戰死者挺立」的不朽意象。

sensitivity.note: The dying-upright at the pillar-stone (the Tain's ending image, and the standing-stone tradition of Cuchulain's memorial) parallels the corpus's standing-deaths (Balor buried standing; the Fianna's foot-to-foot falls); the Morrigan's raven landing on the shoulder closes her feud with the hero. Symbolic pin at the traditional site.

passages.text: And as the day wore on the tide of battle set thicker against Cuchulain; his foes closed in from every side, and though he slew them as they came, his wounds were many, and the death-sickness was upon him. Yet Cuchulain would not fall, for it was not the manner of a hero of the Fianna to fall before his foes while strength was left him; and he made his way to a great pillar-stone that stood hard by, and he set his back against it, and with his belt he bound himself upright to the stone, that he might die as a warrior should, facing his foes, with his weapons in his hand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And there he died, standing up against the pillar-stone, and so terrible was his aspect even in death, that none of his enemies dared to come near him, until at last a raven came and settled upon his shoulder; and then they knew that the Hound of Ulster was no more. And his friends came, and Loeg his charioteer, and they loosed the belt from the stone and bore the body away; and the deeds of Cuchulain were told in Ulster from that day to this, and fame outlived life, and the Red Branch mourned its chief, and the standing-stone at the ford kept the memory of the Hound at Bay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXVIII; not verbatim.
